english: Korean class is more fun than I expected.
tip: 생각보다 (saenggak-boda) is literally 'than thought' – a ready-made 'than I expected'. Korean compares straight against the noun for your expectation, no verb needed.

english: I like winter more than summer.
tip: Preferences reuse the comparison particle: 여름보다 겨울을 좋아해요 (yeoreum-boda gyeoureul joahaeyo) = like winter more than summer. No word for 'more' – 보다 (boda) implies it.

english: Today is less cold than yesterday.
tip: 덜 (deol) is the mirror of 더 (deo): 덜 추워요 (deol chuwoyo) = less cold. English rebuilds the sentence with 'not as cold as'; Korean just swaps in 덜.

english: The soup is less salty than yesterday.
tip: 덜 (deol) = less, dropped right before the adjective: 덜 짜요 (deol jjayo) = less salty. Korean has no '-er' endings – degree words like 덜 and 더 (deo = more) sit before the plain adjective.

english: Please speak a little more slowly.
tip: -어 주세요 = do it for me: 말해 주세요 (malhae juseyo) = please say it.

english: This place's tteokbokki is the best.
tip: 제일 (jeil) in front of an adjective makes the superlative: 제일 맛있어요 (jeil masisseoyo) = the tastiest. Nothing about the adjective changes – the little word does all the work.

target: 우리 팀에서 지은 씨가 노래를 제일 잘해요.
english: Jieun sings the best on our team.
tip: -에서 marks the group for superlatives: 우리 팀에서 (uri tim-eseo) = on our team.

target: 가족 중에서 아빠가 키가 제일 커요.
english: Dad is the tallest in the family.
tip: 중에서 (jung-eseo) scopes a superlative to a group: 가족 중에서 (gajok jung-eseo) = among the family. Without it, 제일 커요 (jeil keoyo) would mean tallest of everyone.

target: 일 년 중에서 오월이 가장 좋아요.
english: May is my favorite month of the year.
tip: 가장 (gajang) and 제일 (jeil) both mean 'most', but 가장 leans slightly formal and written – 가장 좋아요 (gajang joayo) sounds a touch more composed than 제일 좋아요 (jeil joayo).

english: Monday is the busiest day at work.
tip: 제일 (jeil) and 가장 (gajang) both mean 'most' – 제일 is the everyday spoken choice: 제일 바빠요 (jeil bappayo) = is the busiest.

target: 겨울에는 이 온천이 제일 인기가 많아요.
english: In winter this hot spring is the most popular.
tip: Popularity is something you have in Korean: 인기가 많아요 (ingi-ga manayo) is literally 'popularity is much'. Friends work the same way – 친구가 많아요 (chingu-ga manayo).

target: 한 달 중에서 월급날이 제일 좋아요.
english: Payday is the best day of the month.
tip: 월급날 (wolgeumnal) hides a sound shift: the ㅂ (b) of 월급 (wolgeup) turns into ㅁ (m) before the ㄴ (n) of 날 (nal). Korean smooths consonant clashes like this constantly.

english: My little sister sings like a pop star.
tip: 처럼 (cheoreom) means 'like' and glues straight onto the noun: 가수처럼 (gasu-cheoreom) = like a singer. No separate 'as' or 'like' floating in the sentence – the particle carries it.

english: The baby sleeps like an angel.
tip: 처럼 (cheoreom) means 'like' but glues onto the END of its noun: 천사처럼 자요 (cheonsa-cheoreom jayo) = sleeps like an angel. English puts 'like' before – Korean always after.

english: This plate is plastic.
tip: Materials just take the copula: 플라스틱이에요 (peullaseutik-ieyo) = it's plastic.

english: The market alleys are packed every weekend.
tip: 주말마다 (jumal-mada) = every weekend – 마다 (mada) already carries the 'each and every', so the noun never pluralizes: no 'weekends' needed.

english: My grandma's heart is wide as the sea.
tip: 마음이 바다처럼 넓어요 (maeum-i bada-cheoreom neolbeoyo) – a generous heart is 'wide' in Korean, not big. Wide as the sea is the stock image for a forgiving nature.

english: Jieun has long hair.
tip: Describe people with body word + adjective: 머리가 길어요 (meori-ga gireoyo) = has long hair.

english: Minsu is a generous host.
tip: 손이 커요 (son-i keoyo), literally 'has big hands' = cooks and serves generously.

english: Our team lead has a gentle voice.
tip: Respect extends to a person's traits: 부드러우세요 (budeureouseyo) takes the honorific -(으)세요 (-(eu)seyo) because the voice belongs to the 팀장님 (timjangnim). Even their qualities get honored.

target: 아빠는 키가 크고 엄마는 키가 작아요.
english: Dad is tall and Mom is short.
tip: -고 (-go) links sentences: 크고 (keugo) = is tall and…

english: Hello, I'd like to check in.
tip: English loans turn into verbs with 하다 (hada): 체크인하고 싶어요 (chekeuinhago sipeoyo) is literally 'want to do check-in'. The same trick gives 쇼핑하다 (syopinghada) = to shop.

english: I booked under the name Kim Sujin.
tip: (으)로 marks the means: 이름으로 (ireum-euro) = under the name.

english: I'm staying two nights, three days.
tip: Nights and days count with Sino numbers: 2박 3일 (i-bak sam-il) = 2 nights, 3 days.

english: An ocean-view room, please.
tip: 부탁해요 (butakhaeyo) literally asks a favor: 'I entrust this to you'. It turns a bare noun like 방 (bang), room, into a full polite request – no command verb needed.

english: Is breakfast included?
tip: 조식 (josik) is hotel-register breakfast – the formal word you'll meet at check-in and on signs. In everyday talk, breakfast is just 아침 (achim), 'morning'.

english: Checkout is at eleven.
tip: Clock hours use native numbers: 열한 시 (yeolhan si) = eleven o'clock.

english: The pension is right in front of the sea.
tip: 펜션 (pensyeon) is a false friend – in Korea it's a rental holiday guesthouse, a family-trip staple, not a retirement pension. Unlike a hotel room, it usually comes with a kitchen.

english: You can see the sea from the room.
tip: 보이다 = be visible: 바다가 보여요 (bada-ga boyeoyo) = the sea is in view.

target: 일찍 도착했어요. 방이 아직 준비 중이에요.
english: I arrived early. The room is still being prepared.
tip: N 중이에요 = in the middle of N: 준비 중이에요 (junbi jung-ieyo) = being prepared.
